title: How To Make Milk Peda: A Classic Indian Sweet With Mathura Roots
excerpt: This simple recipe uses milk powder and condensed milk to recreate the beloved temple sweet in under 30 minutes, no traditional khoya required.
body:
• Peda — a fudge-like milk sweet made from khoya, sugar, and cardamom — is one of India’s oldest confections, with roots in Mathura, Uttar Pradesh, the birthplace of Lord Krishna.
  • This home-friendly recipe uses milk powder and condensed milk as a shortcut to traditional khoya, yielding soft, melt-in-your-mouth pedas in under 30 minutes.
  • Pedas are an essential offering during Janmashtami and Holi, and remain one of the most popular sweets at Indian grocery stores and mithai shops across the diaspora.

Few Indian sweets carry as much cultural weight as the peda. This dense, fudge-like confection made from slow-cooked milk solids has been part of temple offerings, festival celebrations, and family gift boxes for centuries. Rooted in the holy city of Mathura — Lord Krishna’s birthplace — the peda occupies a space somewhere between dessert and devotion.

While traditional pedas require hours of stirring whole milk down into khoya (dried milk solids), this recipe uses milk powder and condensed milk for a practical home version that captures the same rich, cardamom-scented flavor. The result is ready in about 25 minutes.

Origins: From Temple Offering to National Staple

The peda traces its origins to the Brijwasi community of Mathura and nearby Vrindavan in Uttar Pradesh. According to local tradition, priests devoted to Lord Krishna first prepared the sweet as part of daily temple rituals, using fresh mawa, sugar, and ghee. The sweet’s popularity spread beyond the temple precincts and across India, evolving from a sacred offering into one of the country’s most recognizable confections.

"The sweet is referenced in Indian folklore and devotional songs, including the well-known worship tune “Mathura ke pede mohe lave, khilawe ji” (“bring me the Mathura peda to eat”)."

Mathura peda is so iconic that it functions as a brand name for the entire category. The city’s sweet shops — particularly those near the Shri Krishna Janmabhoomi Temple — attract millions of pilgrims and tourists who carry boxes of peda home as souvenirs. The sweet is referenced in Indian folklore and devotional songs, including the well-known worship tune “Mathura ke pede mohe lave, khilawe ji” (“bring me the Mathura peda to eat”).

Milk Peda Recipe

Prep time: 5 minutes | Cook time: 20 minutes | Makes: 12-14 pedas

Ingredients:

  • 2 cups milk powder (full-fat preferred)
  • 1 can (14 oz / 400g) sweetened condensed milk
  • 2 tablespoons ghee
  • ½ teaspoon cardamom powder
  • A few saffron strands (optional)
  • Chopped pistachios or almonds for garnish

Instructions:

  1. Heat the ghee in a heavy-bottomed or non-stick pan over medium-low heat.
  2. Add the condensed milk and milk powder. Stir continuously to form a smooth paste without lumps.
  3. Cook on medium heat, stirring constantly, for 8-10 minutes. The mixture will thicken and begin to pull away from the sides of the pan.
  4. Add cardamom powder and saffron (if using). Mix well and cook for another minute until the mixture forms a cohesive dough-like mass.
  5. Transfer to a plate and let it cool until warm enough to handle — about 10 minutes.
  6. Shape the pedas: Grease your palms lightly with ghee. Pinch off small portions of the dough, roll into balls, and press gently to flatten into a disc. Make a slight indentation in the center with your thumb.
  7. Garnish with a sliver of pistachio or almond pressed into the center. Let cool completely before serving.

Tips for the Best Pedas

  • Don’t overcook. The mixture will firm up further as it cools. Pull it off the heat when it just starts leaving the sides of the pan, while still slightly moist.
  • Use full-fat milk powder for a creamier texture. Low-fat versions will work but produce a drier peda.
  • Shape while warm. The dough becomes difficult to mold once fully cooled.
  • Storage: Keep in an airtight container at room temperature for up to a week, or refrigerate for up to two weeks.

Variations to Try

The basic peda dough is a canvas for experimentation. Kesar Badam Peda adds saffron soaked in warm milk and slivered almonds. Chocolate Peda folds in a tablespoon of cocoa powder and a splash of vanilla. Paan Peda, popular in North India, mixes in ground betel leaf paste and gulkand (rose petal jam) for a distinctive herbal-floral flavor. Each variation starts with the same base recipe.

A Sweet With Staying Power

For the Indian diaspora, peda is a constant presence — stacked in glass cases at mithai shops from Edison to Southall, offered at pujas and housewarming ceremonies, and exchanged during Diwali along with boxes of barfi and laddu. Its simplicity is part of its staying power: a handful of pantry ingredients, a few minutes of stirring, and a sweet that connects a kitchen in New Jersey to a temple in Mathura. Making it at home brings that connection even closer.
